newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Zinc seen testing $1,300, China sells.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Zinc seen testing $1,300, China sells.

text.p: Robust zinc prices, which hit a fresh 4-1/2 year peak on the London Metal Exchange (LME) overnight, have sparked some Chinese selling and more may be on the way, regional dealers said on Friday.
Zinc advanced to a high of US$1,287 a tonne the London Metal Exchange (LME) and may soon breach the $1,300 level, they said.

"The Chinese are already offering zinc at FOB $20-$40 basis over LME cash. There are people buying because that is still comparatively cheap," a senior dealer for a European metal trading company told Reuters.
"I think the Chinese are thinking of exporting in larger quantities. They'll try to cash in on these high prices," the zinc dealer for a Japanese trading house said.
But another trader was more cautious over the issue of whether Chinese selling would emerge in force.
"I don't know if the current prices are enough for the Chinese. Some of them believe the price has not yet hit its peak and they may wait a bit for that," he said.
Singapore traders said zinc should easily barge past $1,300 a tonne on the LME either today or early next week.
"In the next one to two weeks, the supporting line for zinc will be above $1,300," a dealer for a Japanese trading house said. "Zinc has the strength to push past $1,300."
But metals broker Brandeis cautioned in its daily review on Thursday the market has "moved further into the overbought portion of the chart."
"However, if there is a further drawdown in stocks tomorrow, we cannot rule out a test of $1,300 before a correction is seen," Brandeis said.
One Japanese trader calculated that zinc stocks will probably fall by 2,000-3,000 tonnes when the LME stocks report is released at 0900 GMT.
"That will allow zinc to test $1,300 today," he said.
Business around the region, however, remained a bit subdued except for aluminium, which saw a continuation of strong demand especially from Indonesia, traders said.
"Demand in Indonesia is still going strong. The premiums there are still around $90," a trader for a European metal dealing company said.

Indonesian demand has firmed because several companies who did not sign long-term contracts found themselves short of metal going into the second quarter of the year, Singapore dealers said. Premiums were at $90 a tonne CIF Jakarta.
Strong demand in Japan and Taiwan also kept premiums there high, Singapore dealers said.
Japanese premiums were quoted at $80-$82 a tonne over cash LME prices while Taiwanese premiums were seen at $90 a tonne CIF Kaohsiung.

"If somebody needs the metal, you have to pay the premiums. I don't see the premiums rising any higher, but they are not declining," a trader said, adding this is indicative of demand for aluminium in the region.
"The Japanese are prepared to pay the premiums. The Chinese are also fairly active in buying small lots," he added.
Aluminium buying by India, however, has practically dried up after the Finance Minister recently raise the import duty on the metal to 20 percent from 10 percent.
"India is quiet," one trader said.
Regional demand for copper was quiet as buyers waited for a price correction in prices on the LME.
"The buyers are watching the market because they feel the prices are too high now," a Japanese dealer said.
Three-month copper was quoted by regional dealers at 0200 GMT at $2,331/36 a tonne, little changed from yesterday's late trade in London of $2,332/35 a tonne and down from the kerb close of $2,339.
Singapore premiums for Grade A cathodes were reported easier at $20-$25 a tonne from last week's $25-$35, but trading remained slim, dealers said.
"Even at $20-$25, business is quite difficult," a dealer said.
